description: Conversational learning cards with subtitle, body paragraphs, and takeaway per card.

article.title: The Friendship Paradox: Why Your Friends Have More Friends Than You Do
article.author: Dr. Jennifer Lawson

cards.title: Popular People Are Overrepresented in Friend Groups
cards.subtitle: Your friends probably have more friends than you do—and it's not bad luck, it's math.
body: People with many friends show up in more friend groups. The person with 100 friends gets counted in 100 people's averages. You, with 10 friends, get counted in 10.
Popular nodes are sampled more frequently. So when you average across your friends, you're pulling in a lot of highly connected people.
It's structural, not personal. Your social circle isn't a random sample—it's biased toward people who know a lot of people.
cards.takeaway: Your average friend is more connected than you; that's how the math works out.

cards.title: Reciprocal Friendship Is Rarer Than You Think
cards.subtitle: About half the people you consider close friends may not list you back.
body: Studies find that roughly 50% of perceived friendships aren't reciprocal. You might list twelve close friends; when researchers ask those people, only six might list you.
Friendship is often asymmetric. Your ranking of closeness doesn't necessarily match theirs.
We assume reciprocity more than we confirm it. It's worth being aware that the feeling might not always go both ways.
cards.takeaway: Reciprocity in friendship is assumed more often than it's verified.

cards.title: Dunbar's Number Isn't About Capacity—It's About Time
cards.subtitle: You could remember 500 people, but maintaining that many relationships isn't possible.
body: Dunbar's number—around 150—is often framed as a cognitive limit. But the real constraint is time. Maintaining relationships requires regular interaction.
Memory can hold far more faces and names than you have hours to invest. Relationships decay without input.
You're not brain-limited; you're time-limited. Quality connections need ongoing attention.
cards.takeaway: The limit on relationships is usually time, not how many people you can remember.

cards.title: Proximity Creates Friendships More Than Similarity
cards.subtitle: Your college roommate was randomly assigned; now they're one of your closest friends.
body: Repeated exposure—same classes, same dorm, same office—creates familiarity and liking. Similarity helps, but proximity is often the stronger predictor of who becomes a friend.
Most friendships form from convenience. Who you see regularly shapes who you befriend.
Chance and access matter more than we like to think. Compatibility helps once you're in the same room.
cards.takeaway: Proximity and repeated exposure often matter more than similarity in forming friendships.

cards.title: Weak Ties Provide More Opportunities Than Strong Ones
cards.subtitle: Your best friend knows the same people you do; an acquaintance from a conference got you the job.
body: Strong ties overlap your world. Your close friends often know the same people and information you do.
Weak ties—acquaintances, former colleagues, people from different circles—bridge to different networks. Jobs, ideas, and opportunities often come through them.
Networking isn't mainly about deepening existing bonds; it's about maintaining bridges to other worlds.
cards.takeaway: Weak ties often provide new opportunities that strong ties don't.

cards.title: You Underestimate How Much People Like You After Conversations
cards.subtitle: You thought the conversation was awkward; they thought you were interesting.
body: People consistently underestimate how much others enjoyed talking to them. Researchers call it the 'liking gap.' You assume you made a worse impression than you did.
Others tend to remember you more fondly than you assume. Self-criticism distorts your sense of how you came across.
The gap persists even when you get positive feedback. We're often our own harshest critics.
cards.takeaway: You're probably a worse judge of your impression than the other person is.

cards.title: Relationship Satisfaction Peaks Early and Late
cards.subtitle: Marital satisfaction often follows a U-curve: high early, low in the middle, high again later.
body: The early years of marriage tend to be exciting. Then come the middle years—kids, stress, routine—and satisfaction often drops.
Empty-nest years often see a recovery. The pattern shows up across cultures.
The decline in the middle isn't failure; it's a common structural challenge. Knowing that can help you ride it out.
cards.takeaway: The middle years of long relationships are often the hardest; that's normal.

cards.title: You're More Likely to Marry Someone Geographically Close
cards.subtitle: Statistically, your 'soulmate' probably lived within twenty miles.
body: Most people marry someone from their city, school, or workplace. Destiny, in practice, is often proximity.
The perfect match you never met doesn't count. Geography constrains the pool drastically.
Love can feel fated, but it's also logistically determined. Your soulmate pool is whoever you happened to cross paths with.
cards.takeaway: Geography shapes who we end up with more than we usually acknowledge.

cards.title: Conflict Avoidance Predicts Breakups Better Than Conflict Frequency
cards.subtitle: Couples who never fight often aren't in harmony—they're disengaged.
body: Avoiding conflict can feel like peace. But it often means issues accumulate silently. There's no resolution, just withdrawal.
Couples who argue constructively—and repair afterward—tend to last longer. Engagement, even when it's uncomfortable, maintains connection.
No fighting can mean no caring. Healthy couples disagree and work through it.
cards.takeaway: Conflict avoidance often predicts breakups more than conflict itself.

cards.title: Contempt Is the Strongest Predictor of Divorce
cards.subtitle: Criticism is manageable; contempt—eye rolls, mockery, disgust—is often terminal.
body: Gottman's research identifies contempt as the most toxic behavior in relationships. It signals a loss of respect. You're not just upset; you're treating your partner as beneath you.
Criticism can be addressed. Contempt erodes the foundation. Other conflicts can heal; contempt rarely does.
It's worth watching for—in yourself as much as in your partner.
cards.takeaway: Contempt is the strongest predictor of divorce; it's worth taking seriously.
